list.listitem: Athletes, especially those who are older and exercise sporadically, should be cautioned to stretch before exercise and to rest any joints with tendon pain from overuse or microtrauma. C
Rupture of a tendon should be considered in all injuries where there was a "snap" and sudden pain with an exertional force. C
A history and physical examination can diagnose most tendon ruptures and lacerations, but ultrasonography and MRI improve the accuracy of diagnosis. B
Conservative treatment is indicated for some tendon ruptures such as "mallet finger" or the proximal biceps tendon, and selectively for Achilles tendon rupture, B but most require surgical repair. C
Care must be taken to differentiate between acute traumatic vs. chronic degenerative tendon tears as management and outcomes differ. C

background.definition: Tendons anchor muscle to bone and can be lacerated or ruptured. Tendon ruptures occur at the tendon-bone interface or within the tendon, either from acute tensile overload in healthy tendons or during strenuous movement in tendons weakened by repetitive microtrauma.

list.listitem: Overuse injuries, including tendinopathy, make up nearly 7% of injury-related visits to family physicians. Tendon ruptures are only occasionally seen.

Tendon lacerations, especially in the hand and forearm, occur commonly in deep penetrating lacerations from glass or knives. In a study of small, deep lacerations 55% had at least one tendon injury; of these, 61% of the injuries were to the extensor tendons.
Most hamstring injuries are mild strains, but also moderate and severe injuries occur. Hamstring injuries usually occur in rapid movements involving eccentric demands of the posterior thigh.
Tendon degeneration is believed to contribute to more than 90% of tendon ruptures. Acute trauma, falls, overextension, and blunt trauma can rupture tendons with underlying tendinopathy.
Tendon lacerations are seen in the hand, wrist, and forearm by broken glass, knives, and occupational hazards, such as metal and machines.
An acute tensile overload can rupture healthy tendons (for example, when a running back in football is tackled by more than one person at a time).
Current fluoroquinolone use is associated with an increased risk of tendon rupture (OR = 8.4 for patients older than 60 years).
A systematic review found no consistent evidence of an association between statins and tendon rupture.
Tendon injuries are relatively common in patients with ankle and hindfoot fractures.

Overuse or repetitive microtrauma weakens the collagen cross-linking and noncollagenous matrix of the tendon and decreases its vascularity, resulting in a loss of blood flow, hypoxia, and impaired metabolic activity.
Although the tendon sheath may exhibit some inflammation, the degeneration of the tendon and its slow healing ability are the primary pathology.

Stretching prior to exercise and refraining from intermittent or repetitive overexertion is commonly recommended on the basis of expert opinion. A systematic review found only limited quality evidence and none that supported the practice. C
Specialized training focused on exercise, balance, and body control can help to prevent injuries in elite athletes. B
Avoid steroid injections for tendinopathy and decrease strenuous exercise during—and for 10 days after—the use of fluoroquinolones, especially if the patient is older than 60 years. C
Most tendon ruptures or lacerations can be diagnosed by the patient's inability to flex or extend the joint at the insertion of the tendon. C
There may be a palpable defect where the tendon is missing, and the muscle may be balled near its origin. C
Ultrasound and MRI are helpful in selected patients when the diagnosis is not clear from the clinical examination, and may be helpful for planning surgery. C
MRI should be used selectively for imaging and not replace clinical exam findings as asymptomatic tendon abnormalities are common, especially in older adults. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Pain and ecchymosis over the muscle body
Diffuse tenderness along tendon and at the insertion

list.listitem: Most tendon ruptures occur during strenuous movement (a sudden load against a joint). Patient experiences a sudden, sharp pain, and occasionally an audible snap. Area is tender and ecchymotic, and the balled up muscle and/or a gap in the tendon may be palpated. Loss of the ability to flex or extend the joint at the insertion of the tendon is diagnostic but some flexion or extension may be preserved if other tendons are intact.

Quadriceps and patellar tendon ruptures: The mechanism of injury is usually a direct fall on the knee; patients present with acute knee pain, swelling, bruising, tenderness, and difficulty extending the knee. Patellar tendon rupture is more common in patients younger than 40 years; the patella is displaced superiorly and the defect is palpable below the patella. Quadriceps tendon rupture is more common in patients older than 40 years; the patella is displaced inferiorly and the defect is palpable above the patella.
Posterior tibial tendon rupture: Typically presents from overuse with pain behind the medial malleolus and a flattened, inward canting foot.
Peroneal tendon rupture: Usually occurs in conjunction with an ankle sprain; may present as a sprain that does not heal appropriately.

Biceps tendon rupture: In a proximal biceps tendon rupture the biceps muscle bunches distally creating the classic "Popeye arm." There is minimal loss of function since only one head of the biceps normally ruptures. When the distal biceps tendon is ruptured, the elbow is painful and swollen, with weakness in flexion and supination of the forearm. The sentinel sign is scuffing, abrasion or partial tear anteriorly seen during arthroscopy suggests coexistant subscapularis rupture, but has not been well studied.

Distal biceps tendon rupture: With the Hook test, the patient actively supinates with the elbow at 90 degrees, and the examiner tries to hook an index finger under the lateral side of the biceps tendon. If the finger can hook under the biceps and pull it forward, the result is positive. Proximal biceps tendon rupture: With Ludington's test, the patient is seated with hands behind head, contracts biceps, examiner feels for biceps tendon, its absence indicates rupture.

Finger flexor injury: In flexor tendon rupture, there is tenderness over the flexor aspect of the finger, and the patient is unable to flex at least one of the finger joints. Attempting to do so elicits pain.

Extensor tendon rupture/laceration: Extensor tendon ruptures produce distinctive abnormalities and tenderness over the dorsal aspect of the affected joint. Fixed flexion of the distal interphalangeal joint produces a mallet finger, and fixed flexion at the proximal interphalangeal joint produces the boutonniere deformity. Patients should have a 3-view X-ray of the affected finger. Lacerations involving the tendons on the back of the hand will produce the inability to extend the finger at the metacarpophalangeal joint.
DIP extensor tendon: One common tendon rupture in the hand is the mallet finger, an extensor tendon rupture at the distal interphalangeal joint caused by blunt trauma to the end of the finger.

Infraspinatus tendon tear: The best tests for diagnosing infraspinatus tendon tear in adults are the drop sign and resisted external rotation test (RERT). The best combination of tests is RERT and the Patte sign:
Drop sign: arms is passively elevated to 90 degrees with examiner supporting elbow with hand while rotating the arm to maximal external rotation with the other hand. The patient is asked to hold this position for 10 seconds. The result is considered positive if the arm drops back to internal rotation by more than 5 degrees. RERT test: with the arm at zero degrees of abduction, the elbow at 90 degrees of flexion, and the shoulder at a neutral rotation, the patient is asked to externally rotate the arm against the examiner's resistance, with muscle weakness (not pain alone) considered a positive result. The Patte sign: with the arm at 90 degrees of elevation and 90 degrees of external rotation, and with the elbow at 90 degrees of flexion, the patients is asked to externally rotate the arm against the examiner's resistance. Either pain or weakness is considered a positive test result.
Achilles tendon rupture is discussed in a separate chapter.
Ultrasonography is a valuable tool for the diagnosis of tendon ruptures. In the Achilles tendon, ultrasonography is 72% sensitive and 83% specific.

MRI is useful for the diagnosis of tendon rupture and may decrease unnecessary surgical exploration. However, it should be used selectively as it less accurate in evaluating certain tendons (subscapularis and biceps tendons).
In a series of 58 patients with chronic lateral epicondylitis, ultrasound was 65% sensitive and 85% specific (LR+ 4.3, LR- 0.4) compared with MRI for detection of common extensor tendon tear.

Abnormal tendon findings on imaging are common in asymptomatic individuals especially with increasing age. Tendon abnormalities of the knee were found on MRI in 46% of asymptomatic individuals. The prevalence of rotator cuff tendon pathology has been reported to be 8-40% for partial thickness tears on ultrasound and MRI.
See for a diagnostic algorithm.

Patient compliance should be monitored when treating extensor tendon injuries with splints because the finger must not leave the splint for 6 weeks. All splints for mallet finger show similar results. A
Most tendon ruptures and lacerations are surgically repaired. C
Operative repair and non-operative management of acute Achilles tendon rupture result in comparable patient-reported outcomes. B
Use pain medication as needed. Acetaminophen and NSAIDs usually suffice.

Evidence is inconclusive for the value of injection therapies (including platelet-rich plasma, autologous blood injection, sclerosing agents, corticosteroids among others) for non-insertional achilles tendinosis.
One small RCT found a some benefit to ultrasound guided corticosteroid injection over placebo injection in patients with achilles tendinopathy (unruptured) at 1 to 6 months, but not at 12 months.

Most tendon ruptures in large tendons undergo surgical repair. Achilles tendon rupture can be treated with casting, although most cases are now repaired surgically. A randomized trial with 14 year follow-up compared simple end-to-end repair with fascial flap-augmented repair in 55 patients with Achilles tendon rupture, and found no difference in outcomes. Both groups had persistent weakness on the affected side.
A randomized trial found that operative repair and non-operative management of acute Achilles tendon rupture result in comparable patient-reported outcomes.

A 2022 Norwegian RCT randomized 554 adults age 18 to 60 with acute Achilles tendon rupture to non-operative management, open repair, and minimally invasive surgery. The nonoperative management involved a below-the-knee equinus cast for 2 weeks, followed by 6 weeks of weight-bearing as tolerated with heel wedges and ankle-foot orthoses. Patients had gradually decreasing plantar flexion with progressive removal of heel lifts in the 6 weeks following the equinus cast. The brace was worn day and night for the first 2 weeks but was removed at night for weeks 2 through 6. At 1 year, there was no difference in the primary outcome of a change in the Achilles tendon Total Rupture Score compared with baseline status pre-injury: -17 points for nonoperative treatment, -16 points for open repair, and - 14.7 points for minimally invasive surgery. Nerve injuries were less common with nonoperative management (0.6% vs 2.8% with open repair and 5.2% with minimally invasive surgery). However, re-ruptures were more common with nonoperative management (6.2% vs 0.6% in each of the surgery groups, number needed to treat to harm = 18), with most occurring in the 10 weeks following the index injury.
Surgery is indicated for rupture of the quadriceps, patellar, hamstrings, and distal biceps tendons. Repair of the posterior tibial tendon may require a tendon transfer.

Most complete lacerations of the extensor and flexor tendons in the hand and forearm are surgically repaired. Best results for repair of lacerations of flexor tendons in the hand occur in sharp lacerations when repair is made early and the A2 and A4 pulleys are preserved.
A systematic review of cases of tibialis anterior tendon rupture found that most patients (72 of 87) were treated surgically. Older patients were more likely to undergo conservative management.
Conservative treatment of mallet finger by splinting the finger in slight hyperextension is safe and effective for at least 80% of patients.
Distal biceps tendon rupture treatment is usually operative. Different fixation techniques have been applied to athletes, with high success rates.

Most hamstring injuries are treated non-surgically with good results. However, there are clear indications for surgical treatment, such as severe tendon avulsions. Surgical treatment has been found to have good results in severe injuries, especially if the avulsion injury is repaired in the acute phase.

There was a high rate of return to sport (RTS) after distal biceps tendon repair at 6 months postoperatively. A positive trend for RTS was observed with respect to rehabilitation protocols favoring earlier active mobility.
Massage subjectively loosens muscles and decreases pain but has no supporting evidence.
Dietary supplementation of protein or the primary amino acids found in tendons (glycine, lysine, and proline) has no supporting evidence.
The use of stem cells and specific growth factors to enhance repair of tendons may be treatments in the future.
Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections were no better than placebo injections in improving pain or function in patients with nonsurgically treated acute Achilles tendon ruptures.

This was also the conclusion of a trial randomizing 230 patients with acute complete Achilles tendon rupture to PRP or dry needle insertion. At the end of the study pain and function were similar between groups.

Extensor tendon ruptures at the proximal interphalangeal or distal interphalangeal joints that are not associated with an avulsion fracture involving more than 30% of the joint may be managed in a finger splint that keeps the injured joint in full extension for 6 weeks.
Posterior tibial tendon ruptures may be treated with orthotic arch supports.
A rupture of the proximal head of the biceps is repaired only in active young people. Since there are 2 origins, the loss of 1 is not generally functionally significant.

Rehabilitation is encouraged after surgery for tendon repair. Structurally strong repairs are made to allow for early mobility and physical therapy. Most patients undergoing surgical repair for ruptured tendons benefit from early mobilization with no evidence available for superiority of active (only in carefully selected patients) or passive motion.
Conservative treatment of mallet finger by splinting the finger in slight hyperextension is safe and effective for at least 80% of patients.

Immediate mobilization after repair of Achilles tendon rupture may increase the incidence of re-rupture. Consider the use of accelerated rehabilitation intervention in early postoperative rehabilitation of the Achilles tendon.

Low-certainty evidence from a single trial in people with lateral elbow pain indicates that manual therapy may provide a clinically worthwhile benefit in terms of pain and disability at the end of treatment for lateral elbow pain.
Exercise therapy with a focus on eccentric strengthening is the most effective treatment for many forms of tendinopathy.
Relative rest, ice, compression, and elevation can be used as symptomatic therapy for any tendon injury.

A UK study randomized adults with acute Achilles tendon rupture who chose not to have surgery to a functional brace (n = 274) or below knee plaster cast for 8 weeks (n = 266). Outcomes were similar between groups.

Patients with acute Achilles tendon rupture treated non-operatively have comparable functional outcomes whether they are managed with plaster casts followed by rehabilitation or walking boots followed by rehabilitation.

Both PRP (platelet rich plasma) and corticosteroid (CS) injections may be effective treatments for patients with lateral epicondylopathy. A systematic review identified 7 RCTs with 730 patients comparing CS injection with PRP injection (there were no placebo groups) Corticosteroid injection provides better short-term (<2 months) functional improvement and may be more advantageous in terms of short-term pain relief, while PRP provides better long-term (≥6 months) functional improvement and better performance regarding long-term pain relief.

Percutaneous needle tenotomy is a safe, beneficial, and minimally invasive treatment option for patients with tendinopathy, especially for conditions refractory to more conservative treatments options.
In a series of 52 patients, 96% achieved a good or excellent outcome after repair of acute Achilles tendon ruptures.
In a series of 23 patients with biceps tendon rupture followed up for a median of 26 months, more than 90% were satisfied with their repair and returned to their pre-injury occupation.
The incidences of ACL graft rupture and/or clinical failure at more than 10 years after ACL reconstruction are 6.2% and 10.3%, respectively.
Negative prognostic factors for acute Achilles tendon rupture include increasing age (especially over 40 years), co-morbid deep vein thrombosis, and male sex.

cell.label: Patient presents with acute swelling at or near a joint.
History of chronic pain and/or steroid injections in that area, or history of fluroquinolone use?
Sudden onset of sharp pain with signs of tendon rupture (unable to flex or extend the joint, balled up muscles, or palpable gap in the tendon?
Tendon rupture; refer to orthopedic surgeon.
Suspect tendinopathy or peritendonitis; consider ultrasound or MRI.
Suspect sprain, fracture, or ligament tear. Take X-rays and ligament tests.
